analysis.one_liner: Bans data brokers from selling Americans' sensitive personal data to China, Russia, Iran, or North Korea.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 414-0, but the Senate Commerce Committee never acted on it, so the bill died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it illegal for data brokers — companies that collect and sell information about people they never met — to sell Americans' sensitive data to China, Russia, Iran, or North Korea, or to companies controlled by those countries. The covered data includes Social Security numbers, financial account details, health records, biometric and genetic data, precise location information, and private messages. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the ban. The House passed it unanimously, but the Senate never voted on it, and the bill died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday Americans whose sensitive personal data is currently collected, packaged, and sold by data brokers: Social Security numbers, health and mental-health records, precise location histories, biometric and genetic information, and private communications would be barred from sale to the four designated adversary countries or entities they control. The FTC would gain a new tool to penalize brokers that sell that data abroad.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal offense for a data broker to sell, rent, trade, or disclose personally identifiable sensitive data — Social Security numbers, financial account details, health records, biometric and genetic data, precise location, private messages — to North Korea, China, Russia, Iran, or entities controlled by those countries.
Covers entities with as little as 20 percent ownership by a foreign adversary's nationals and lets the Federal Trade Commission enforce the ban with civil penalties.
Defines the scope broadly enough to include precise location data accurate to within 1,850 feet, meaning brokers could no longer sell movement histories to foreign-controlled firms.

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers, which would lose a paying customer for sensitive Americans' data, and any foreign-controlled firms buying that data. Companies that collect data directly from users (like major tech platforms) are largely excluded from the ban, so the cost falls on the broker industry specifically.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers selling to foreign buyers

drawbacks.text: The bill only restricts the sale of sensitive data to four named countries; it does nothing to limit the data broker industry's ongoing collection and sale of the same information to domestic buyers, so the underlying privacy problem remains.
Enforcement relies entirely on the Federal Trade Commission; there is no private right of action for individuals whose data is sold, so violations depend on the agency bringing cases.
Entities that collect data directly from individuals and only resell brokered data fall outside the definition of a data broker, leaving potential gaps in coverage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real protection for Americans' most sensitive personal data — Social Security numbers, health records, locations, private messages — from sale to adversarial governments, with essentially no downside for ordinary people. The main limitation is that it is narrow: it stops the foreign sale but does nothing to restrict the data broker industry's ordinary collection and sale practices domestically, or the government's own access to brokered data.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by a unanimous 414-0 vote, but it was sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never considered it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced March 5, 2024, the bill cleared the House Energy and Commerce Committee two days later with a 50-0 vote to report it.

On March 20, 2024, the House passed the bill under a suspension-of-the-rules procedure (a fast-track path requiring two-thirds support) by a vote of 414-0, with every Democrat and Republican voting yes.
The Senate received the bill on March 21, 2024 and referred it to its Commerce Committee, which took no further action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers and any foreign buyers of Americans' sensitive data are better off; the ban never took effect, so their data trade continues as before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers and foreign data buyers

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
for.role: Ranking Member, House Energy and Commerce (sponsor)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and guided it through committee markup and House passage.

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill unanimously (50-0 committee vote) two days after introduction.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the House-passed bill on March 21, 2024 and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was completely bipartisan: all 202 Democrats and all 212 Republicans voting in the House voted yes, and the Senate referred it to a committee controlled by the president's own party where it stalled.

industries.note: Loses a paying customer: foreign adversary-controlled entities can no longer legally buy Americans' Social Security numbers, health data, location trails, and private communications. Their broader domestic business is untouched, however.

industries.industry: Advertising technology and consumer data platforms
industries.note: Firms that collect data directly from users rather than reselling brokered data are excluded from the ban, so many large platforms are largely unaffected; those acting as data brokers face new FTC-enforced restrictions on foreign sales.
